recent_posts.title: Git Workflows Are Broken — Here's What Actually Works at Scale
recent_posts.summary: An experienced engineer breaks down why Git Flow and pure trunk-based development both fail at scale, then proposes a practical hybrid: short-lived feature branches (max 48 hours), mandatory CI gates under 10 minutes, single-reviewer squash merges, deployment gates instead of release branches, and a revert-first culture. The approach prioritizes small atomic changes, fast feedback loops, and clean linear history on main to make rollbacks safe and reliable.

recent_posts.title: PostgreSQL Tips That Senior DBAs Don't Share (Until You Buy Them a Beer)
recent_posts.summary: A collection of advanced PostgreSQL techniques from 12 years of production experience. Covers proper use of EXPLAIN with ANALYZE/BUFFERS/FORMAT JSON for query analysis, partial indexes for performance gains, CTE materialization behavior changes since PG12, pg_stat_statements for identifying slow queries, LISTEN/NOTIFY for real-time pub/sub without polling, GENERATED ALWAYS AS for computed columns, advisory locks for lightweight coordination, and PgBouncer connection pooling as often the biggest performance win.

recent_posts.title: Stop Writing Try-Catch Everywhere — Use Result Types Instead
recent_posts.summary: Exceptions in TypeScript hide failure modes from function signatures, leading to either catch-all handlers that lose context or unhandled errors that crash processes. The Result type pattern — borrowed from Rust — encodes success and failure directly in the return type, making all possible errors visible to callers and the TypeScript compiler. A minimal 4-line type definition enables exhaustive error handling via switch statements, eliminates unexpected throws, and improves composability. The pattern is best suited for expected failures like network errors or missing records, while true exceptions remain appropriate for programming bugs and assertion failures.

recent_posts.title: The "Golden Path" Fallacy: Why Your Team's Best Practices Are Holding You Back
recent_posts.summary: Mature engineering orgs often create 'golden paths' — standardized stacks and processes meant to reduce overhead and enforce consistency. But these can become 'golden cages' that slow teams down, tax innovation, and deliver only surface-level uniformity. A simple internal tool that could ship in 3 days instead takes 6 weeks due to mandatory stack requirements and review processes. The alternative: replace prescriptions with outcome-based principles, adopt Netflix's 'paved road' model (make the standard easy but not mandatory), allocate innovation budgets for off-path experiments, and regularly re-evaluate the path itself. The root issue is often a lack of trust in engineers to make good technology decisions — and golden paths hide that problem rather than solving it.

recent_posts.title: I Mass-Deleted My NPM Dependencies and My App Got Faster — Here's the Full Audit Process
recent_posts.summary: A practical walkthrough of auditing and slimming down a production React app's dependencies. Starting from 1,847 packages and a 2.3MB gzipped bundle, the author used depcheck and bundle visualizer tools to identify unused, redundant, and oversized packages. The process involved removing dead dependencies (moment, axios, lodash), replacing heavy libraries with lighter alternatives or native APIs, and lazy-loading infrequently used modules. The result: 891 packages, 940KB bundle, 6-second builds, and a Lighthouse performance score jump from 62 to 89. The post also covers verification steps after each removal and CI guardrails to prevent future bloat.

recent_posts.title: Docker in 2026: The 5 Mistakes Still Killing Your Containers in Production
recent_posts.summary: Five persistent Docker mistakes still found in production environments in 2026: running containers as root (fix: add a non-root user in Dockerfile), using 'latest' image tags (fix: pin exact versions), bloated single-stage images with build dependencies (fix: multi-stage builds), missing health checks (fix: add HEALTHCHECK instruction), and ignoring .dockerignore (fix: exclude node_modules, .git, .env, etc.). A bonus warning advises against using docker-compose in production, recommending proper orchestration instead. Each mistake includes a concrete Dockerfile snippet or config example.

recent_posts.title: Every Codebase Has a "Room of Shame" — Here's What's Usually In It
recent_posts.summary: A collection of real-world horror stories from production codebases, including a 47,000-line JSON config file, a function with 31 parameters including triple-negation booleans, a try-catch swallowing payment errors for two years, and a zombie microservice costing $400/month that nobody remembered creating. The underlying causes are explored: time pressure, context loss, fear of change, and organizational incentives that reward shipping over maintenance. The takeaway is that every codebase has a 'room of shame' and the best teams schedule dedicated time to address it rather than pretending it doesn't exist.

recent_posts.title: The Tech Stack Doesn't Matter — Your Ability to Ship Does
recent_posts.summary: Teams often waste months debating tech stack choices while solo developers with simpler tools ship products and gain real users. The core argument: for 90% of projects, technology choice is irrelevant to success. What matters is deployment speed, team familiarity, and iterating on real user feedback. Key principles include investing in CI/CD over architecture debates, choosing boring reliable infrastructure (PostgreSQL, monoliths, server-side rendering), and avoiding premature microservices complexity. The guiding question for any tech decision should be: 'Will this help us ship to users faster?'

recent_posts.title: AI Won't Replace Developers — But Developers Using AI Will Replace Those Who Don't
recent_posts.summary: A developer shares a year of experience integrating AI coding tools into their workflow, arguing that AI won't replace developers but will create a divide between those who use it effectively and those who don't. AI excels at boilerplate, tests, and documentation but fails at architectural decisions, business context, and ambiguous requirements. The real risk is junior developers over-relying on AI without understanding fundamentals. The competitive edge goes to engineers who can critically validate AI output, ask better questions, and focus on human-centric skills like communication and architecture. The prediction: AI tools will become as standard as IDEs, and the key skill will be critical thinking about AI-generated code, not just prompting ability.

recent_posts.title: How Tinder Built an API Gateway to Handle a Billion Swipes a Day
recent_posts.summary: Tinder built TAG (Tinder API Gateway), a custom framework handling over a billion daily swipes. Built on Spring Cloud Gateway, TAG allows teams to run their own gateway instances using shared configuration-driven components. The system handles geolocation checks, schema scanning, session validation, and service discovery through a multi-step request pipeline. This approach provides team autonomy while maintaining consistency in authentication, logging, and security across hundreds of microservices.
